book.title: Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach
book.description: The opening arc of modern AI: what intelligence means, how rational agents are designed, and how search turns goals into actions in single-agent, complex, and adversarial worlds.

chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.focus: Definitions of AI, rational action, the intellectual foundations and history of the field, present capabilities, and the benefits and risks of building intelligent systems.
equation: a* = arg max_a E[U(outcome) | evidence, a]

An intelligent system should choose the action with the greatest expected usefulness given what it currently knows. The equation separates evidence, uncertainty, possible consequences, and values; it does not claim that the system knows the world perfectly.
chapters.story: A hospital asks for an AI triage assistant. A dazzling language demo is not yet a specification: the team must decide whether the system imitates clinicians, predicts diagnoses, reasons correctly, or chooses actions that improve patient outcomes under explicit safety constraints.
concepts: Four views of artificial intelligence

AI can be organized around thinking humanly, acting humanly, thinking rationally, or acting rationally. The axes expose different evidence requirements: imitation, cognitive fidelity, logical validity, and successful action are not interchangeable.
The rational-agent view

A rational agent selects actions expected to achieve its goals from the percept history and available knowledge. Rationality is bounded by information and computation; it is not omniscience or guaranteed success.
Foundations across disciplines

Philosophy contributes questions about mind and action; mathematics supplies logic, probability, optimization, and computation; economics adds preferences and decisions; neuroscience and psychology inform learning and cognition; control theory contributes feedback.
Cycles of ambition and correction

AI history alternates between strong ideas, inflated promises, difficult counterexamples, funding contractions, and renewed progress from better algorithms, data, and hardware. The pattern teaches skepticism toward benchmark extrapolation.
Capability, benefit, and risk

A system's technical competence does not determine whether its goal is appropriate. Safety requires attention to specification, uncertainty, misuse, unequal impact, loss of control, and institutions that decide where automation has authority.
pitfalls: Equating fluent imitation with general intelligence
Calling an action rational without stating the objective
Treating benchmark success as proof of safe deployment
Describing AI history as one smooth line of progress
practice: Classify five AI systems using the four historical views
Write a utility table for the triage assistant
Create a timeline linking one advance to its enabling assumption
Perform a benefit-risk-authority review for one deployed AI system

chapters.title: Intelligent Agents
chapters.focus: Agents and environments, rationality, PEAS task specifications, environment properties, reflex and model-based architectures, goals, utilities, learning agents, and safe task design.
equation: Agent as a mapping from history to action

The abstract agent function maps the complete percept history to an action. An implemented program approximates that function using internal state, a model, goals, utility, and learned knowledge on a particular architecture.
chapters.story: Consider a warehouse robot at a crowded packing station. It sees partial camera views, receives delayed inventory updates, shares aisles with people, and must trade speed against collision risk. Saying 'move boxes efficiently' hides nearly every design decision.
concepts: PEAS as a task contract
Performance measure, Environment, Actuators, and Sensors force a vague product request into observable terms. A bad performance measure can make competent optimization produce unwanted behavior.
Environment dimensions

Fully versus partially observable, deterministic versus stochastic, episodic versus sequential, static versus dynamic, discrete versus continuous, and single- versus multiagent properties determine which internal machinery is necessary.
Reflex and model-based agents
A simple reflex maps the current percept to an action. A model-based agent maintains hidden state so it can act when the present observation does not reveal everything relevant.
Goals and utility
Goals distinguish success from failure; utility ranks competing successful states and expresses tradeoffs. Expected utility is essential when actions have uncertain outcomes.
Learning-agent anatomy

A performance element acts, a critic evaluates, a learning element improves behavior, and a problem generator encourages informative exploration. Keeping these roles distinct clarifies feedback and failure.
pitfalls: Writing an agent architecture before defining PEAS
Assuming the latest percept contains the whole state
Using a reward that can be gamed
Confusing rationality with moral acceptability
practice: Write PEAS descriptions for a taxi and a tutoring agent
Classify both environments along every standard dimension
Convert three reflex rules into a stateful design
Identify reward-hacking paths in a warehouse objective

chapters.title: Solving Problems by Searching
chapters.focus: Problem formulation, state spaces, tree and graph search, breadth-first and depth-first search, uniform-cost search, iterative deepening, best-first search, A*, heuristics, and search evaluation.
equation: The path cost g records what has already been paid; the heuristic h estimates the remaining cost. With an admissible heuristic A* tree search is optimal, while graph-search guarantees require the stronger consistency condition or careful reopening of states.
chapters.story: A rescue planner must route a vehicle through flooded streets. The physical city is not the search space by itself: the state must include everything that changes future options, while the action model, goal test, and path cost must reflect safety and time.
concepts: Problem formulation

A search problem specifies initial state, actions, transition model, goal test, and path cost. Omitting relevant history merges states that should behave differently; including irrelevant detail makes search needlessly large.
Tree search versus graph search

Tree search may rediscover the same state through many paths. Graph search stores explored states and frontier information, trading memory for duplicate control and often changing completeness guarantees.
Uninformed strategies

Breadth-first, depth-first, uniform-cost, depth-limited, and iterative deepening order the frontier differently. Their completeness, optimality, time, and space depend on branching, solution depth, and step costs.
Heuristic best-first search

Greedy search follows estimated distance to the goal; A* combines distance already traveled with estimated distance remaining. A heuristic is useful when it is informative and cheap enough to justify its computation.
Admissibility and consistency
Admissibility means never overestimating true remaining cost. Consistency applies a triangle inequality across transitions, making f-values nondecreasing and simplifying correct graph search.
pitfalls: Checking goals only after expanding a node without understanding the strategy
Using breadth-first search when step costs differ
Marking a state closed too early in inconsistent A*
Comparing node counts without counting heuristic cost
practice: Formulate the flooded-city state space
Trace BFS, DFS, UCS, greedy, and A* on one graph
Prove a proposed heuristic admissible or find a counterexample
Measure frontier size as well as solution cost

chapters.title: Search in Complex Environments
chapters.focus: Local search, hill climbing, simulated annealing, local beam search, evolutionary search, continuous optimization, nondeterministic actions, partial observability, online search, and unknown environments.
equation: A worse move with energy increase ΔE may be accepted while temperature T is high, allowing escape from local optima. As T decreases, behavior becomes greedier. The schedule is part of the algorithm, not a decorative parameter.
chapters.story: A university must build a conflict-free timetable with rooms, lecturers, accessibility constraints, preferences, and last-minute changes. The path to a timetable is irrelevant; only the final configuration matters, and the combinatorial space makes systematic path search impractical.
concepts: Local search on complete states

Local methods keep one or a small population of candidate solutions and move through neighboring configurations. Their low memory is attractive for optimization, but they can lose the path and completeness guarantees.
Landscape pathologies
Local maxima, plateaus, ridges, and deceptive basins explain why a locally improving rule may stop far from a good global solution. Restarts and stochastic moves change exploration.
Population and evolutionary search
Beam search shares information among candidates; evolutionary methods select, recombine, and mutate a population. Representation and variation operators determine which regions are reachable.
Nondeterministic and partially observable search
When actions have multiple outcomes or state is hidden, a solution becomes a conditional plan over belief states rather than one fixed action sequence.
Online search and exploration
An online agent interleaves acting and learning because the map is unknown. It must pay real action costs while discovering the transition structure, making exploration a core decision problem.
pitfalls: Reporting the best stochastic run only
Using a neighborhood that disconnects the feasible space
Treating a belief state as one guessed physical state
Ignoring the real cost of online exploration
practice: Implement hill climbing with random restarts for timetabling
Compare two annealing schedules across many seeds
Write an AND-OR plan for a nondeterministic vacuum world
Map exploration regret in a small unknown maze

chapters.title: Adversarial Search and Games
chapters.focus: Game trees, minimax, alpha-beta pruning, move ordering, cutoff search, evaluation functions, Monte Carlo tree search, stochastic games, partial observability, and multiplayer settings.
equation: V(s) = max_a V(Result(s,a)) for MAX; min_a V(Result(s,a)) for MIN

Minimax assumes optimal opposition and backs terminal utilities through alternating choices. It computes the best guaranteed outcome under the model, not the most likely outcome against an imperfect real opponent.
chapters.story: A defensive cyber agent chooses which service to isolate while an attacker chooses where to move next. Each side changes the other's future options. A plan that ignores response is not merely incomplete—it optimizes the wrong world.
concepts: Games as contingent search
A game state includes player to move, legal actions, transitions, terminal tests, and utilities. The solution is a strategy specifying an action for every reachable opponent response.
Minimax and zero-sum assumptions

MAX chooses the child with highest backed-up value while MIN chooses the lowest. The elegant recurrence relies on two-player, deterministic, perfect-information, zero-sum assumptions that must be checked.
Alpha-beta pruning

Alpha is MAX's best guaranteed value; beta is MIN's. A branch can be skipped when it cannot affect the ancestor decision. Good move ordering changes effective search depth dramatically without changing the exact result.
Cutoffs and evaluation
Real games are too large for terminal search. A cutoff replaces terminal utility with a learned or designed evaluation, introducing horizon effects and making feature calibration central.
Monte Carlo tree search
MCTS balances selection, expansion, simulation or value estimation, and backup. Upper-confidence rules trade exploiting known strong moves against exploring uncertain ones.
pitfalls: Applying minimax where utilities are not zero-sum
Claiming alpha-beta changes the optimal move
Evaluating agents only against copies of themselves
Letting rollout bias masquerade as strategic depth
practice: Back up a small game tree by hand
Trace alpha and beta bounds with two move orderings
Design and ablate a cutoff evaluation
Compare minimax and MCTS under fixed computation
